categories: Who is paid by the state

terms.term: Verdict: supported, partly supported, not supported, answered, can't be tested
terms.short: How a claim fared against the official numbers under the rule printed beside it.
terms.long: Each claim on the Questions pages is stated the way it is commonly put and tested with a rule written in plain words (for example 'supported if the top 1% pay at least 25% of income tax'). 'Supported' and 'not supported' mean the numbers meet or miss that rule. 'Partly supported' means some of the claim holds. 'Answered' is for factual questions where the numbers are the answer. 'Can't be tested' means no open data can answer it, and the reason is given.
terms.not_this: A verdict is not a judgement about whether something is good or bad, fair or unfair, and it is only as good as the rule and the data. Change the rule and the verdict can change; the rule is always shown.

terms.short: The date or year a figure describes, which differs between sources.
terms.long: Every source describes a different moment. The census describes March 2021. Universal Credit counts describe May 2026, PIP July 2026, most other benefits March 2026. Council spending is the latest financial year each council has submitted. Tax distribution is the 2023-24 survey year with later years projected. The Data years page lists the period of every source, and each figure on the site names its period. Figures from different periods should not be added or subtracted without saying so.
terms.not_this: Two numbers side by side are not necessarily from the same year, even on the same page.

terms.short: A year running 1 April to 31 March; '2025-26' is April 2025 to March 2026.
terms.long: UK public finances, council budgets and tax statistics use financial years. 2025-26 runs from 6 April or 1 April 2025 to 5 April or 31 March 2026 depending on the source (tax years start on 6 April).

terms.term: Outturn, forecast, projection, plan and budget
terms.short: Outturn is what actually happened; the others are expectations.
terms.long: Outturn is spending or income recorded after the year ended (the first outturn is provisional and gets revised). A budget or plan is what was intended before. A forecast or projection is a statistician's or the OBR's estimate of the future. Charts here draw forecast years with a dashed line and say so.
terms.not_this: A forecast is not data. The OBR's own forecasts have been revised many times.

terms.short: A figure we calculated from published numbers, not one an official body published.
terms.long: Some figures here are our own calculations and are labelled as such. 'Apportioned' means a published total for one area (such as a council's spending) is split among smaller areas (constituencies) in proportion to something else (residents). 'Annualised' means a count at one date multiplied by an average payment and by 52 weeks (or 12 months), so it shows the yearly rate at that date, not cash paid in a financial year. Both can differ from official totals; where an official total exists we show the comparison.
terms.not_this: An estimate for a constituency is not a published constituency figure.

terms.short: Official statistics round small numbers and hide tiny ones to protect privacy.
terms.long: DWP rounds counts (to the nearest 5 in small areas) and Census counts are adjusted slightly for confidentiality. Percentages calculated from small counts are less reliable. A blank means the value was too small to publish or not available, not zero.

terms.short: How closely two measures move together across places, from −1 to 1; it does not show cause.
terms.long: A correlation of 0.8 between two measures across constituencies means places that are high on one tend to be high on the other. A correlation of 0 means no pattern. It describes places, not people, and does not show that one thing causes the other.
terms.not_this: Never read it as 'people in group X do Y'. Area patterns can be driven by something else (age, housing costs, health) entirely.

terms.short: A pattern across areas says nothing certain about the people inside them.
terms.long: Census make-up (religion, ethnicity, country of birth) and benefit counts come from different sources that cannot be linked person by person. Showing that areas with more of one group have more of some benefit would be an association between places, and would be misleading if used to say what any group receives or costs. The site does not link benefit spending to religion, ethnicity or country of birth for that reason.

terms.short: A count divided by a population, so places of different size can be compared.
terms.long: 'PIP cases per 100 aged 15 to 64' divides the number of PIP cases by the Census 2021 population aged 15 to 64 and multiplies by 100. Rates use the 2021 population, so places whose population has grown since are slightly overstated. Each rate names its denominator.

terms.short: The median is the middle value; the mean is the total divided by the number.
terms.long: The median is the figure with half the people above and half below. The mean ('average') adds everything and divides, so a few very large values pull it up. Where a few large values exist (payments to head offices) the site uses medians.

terms.short: Positions in an ordered list: rank 1 is highest; a tercile is a third; a decile a tenth.
terms.long: Rank 1 is the highest value among all the places compared. A percentile splits people into 100 equal groups ordered by income; the 'top 1%' are the 1 in 100 with the highest. A tercile is a third of areas ordered by something (such as deprivation); a decile is a tenth.

terms.term: Kinds of payment: contributory, means-tested, disability and care-need, universal
terms.short: Different payments exist for different reasons; they should not be lumped together as 'welfare'.
terms.long: Contributory payments (State Pension, contribution-based ESA) are earned through National Insurance contributions and paid regardless of income. Means-tested payments (Universal Credit, Pension Credit, Housing Benefit) top up low incomes and fall as other income rises. Disability and care-need payments (PIP, DLA, Attendance Allowance, Carer's Allowance) help with extra costs of illness, disability or caring, mostly whatever the person's income or whether they work. Each has its own rules set by Parliament.
terms.not_this: The word 'benefits' covers pensions, help with disability costs and low-income top-ups alike; most spending goes to pensioners (see the benefits-by-age claim).

terms.short: Who or what is being counted differs by benefit.
terms.long: A 'case' or 'claimant' is one award. For Universal Credit people ('claimants') are counted separately from households (one household can have two adults), and the payment is made per household. 'In payment' means currently being paid; 'with entitlement' means awarded, including a few not currently paid. Counts are for a single date (a snapshot), not everyone who claimed at any time in the year.

terms.term: Benefit spend by area (our annualised estimate)
terms.short: Cases in the area times the average award times 52 (or households times the monthly payment times 12).
terms.long: DWP publishes counts and average awards for each constituency and authority, but not total pounds paid. We multiply the count at the latest date by the average weekly award and by 52 (Universal Credit: households × average monthly payment × 12). That is the yearly rate at that date. Nationally it is compared with DWP's own expenditure for the nearest financial year (see the check table); the two differ because caseloads grow, awards are uprated each April, and some cases are nil-payment.
terms.not_this: It is not cash paid in a financial year, and it is not what any one person receives. It excludes tax credits, Child Benefit, Winter Fuel Payment and other payments not loaded. State Pension paid to people living abroad (about 1.1 million) belongs to no area: it is shown separately and included only in the national comparison with DWP.
used_by: Personal Independence Payment: annualised spend (our estimate)
Disability Living Allowance: annualised spend (our estimate)
Employment and Support Allowance: annualised spend (our estimate)

terms.short: Means-tested payments depend on income and savings; the others do not.
terms.long: Universal Credit, Pension Credit and Housing Benefit are means-tested: they are reduced as income or savings rise. State Pension, PIP, DLA, Attendance Allowance and (for the rate) Carer's Allowance are not means-tested, so people who also work or have savings can receive them.

terms.short: A monthly payment for people on a low income, in or out of work, that replaced six older benefits.
terms.long: Universal Credit is paid per household each month to help with living costs for people who are out of work or on a low income. It replaced Income Support, income-based Jobseeker's Allowance, income-related ESA, Housing Benefit, Child Tax Credit and Working Tax Credit. Households can include people who are working, people who cannot work because of health or caring, parents of young children, and people looking for work.
terms.why_paid: The payment is built from elements for the household's circumstances: a basic allowance for adults; extra for each child (and for a disabled child); help with rent for renters; a carer element; and an element for people assessed as having limited capability for work (because of illness or disability). The household's earnings and savings then reduce it. A higher payment therefore reflects a bigger need (more children, higher rent, disability or caring), not a more generous decision about the person.
terms.who: Adults on a low income or not working: this includes many who are in work (about a quarter in the May 2026 data), people assessed as unable to work because of health or disability, carers, and parents of very young children, as well as people searching for work (about 1 in 5).
terms.amount: Set by the elements above and reduced by earnings (the 'taper'); average monthly amounts per household are in the data.
terms.avoid_blame: Most people on Universal Credit are not in the 'searching for work' group. Being on UC is not the same as being out of work, and being in the 'no work requirements' group is a rule-based result of health, caring or a very young child, not a choice.
used_by: People on Universal Credit, per 100 aged 15 to 64
UC claimants with no work requirements (health, disability, caring, young children)
UC claimants in the 'searching for work' group
UC claimants with a health condition (limited capability for work)
Share of UC claimants with a health condition

terms.short: The group DWP assigns each UC claimant to, which sets what job-related activity is expected of them.
terms.long: Searching for work: expected to look for and prepare for work. Working, with requirements: in work but earning below the level where requirements stop, so must try to increase earnings. Working, no requirements: earning enough that no further requirements apply. Planning for work and Preparing for work: expected to take steps towards work in future (for example a parent of a young child, or someone with limited capability for work who may be able to prepare). No work requirements: not expected to look for work because of, for example, limited capability for work and work-related activity (severe illness or disability), caring for a severely disabled person full-time, or looking after a very young child.
terms.not_this: 'No work requirements' does not mean 'not working' or 'refusing to work'. It is a legal category based on health, caring or young children, and some people in it also have earnings.

terms.term: Limited capability for work (LCW) and for work-related activity (LCWRA)
terms.short: A result of the Work Capability Assessment: a health condition or disability limits the work someone can be expected to do.
terms.long: DWP assesses whether a health condition or disability limits someone's ability to work (limited capability for work) or to prepare for work (limited capability for work-related activity, the more severe level). The result decides whether someone on Universal Credit or ESA has work requirements and receives an extra amount.
terms.not_this: It is based on how a condition affects what a person can do, not on a diagnosis, and people are reassessed.

terms.short: A payment towards the extra costs of a long-term health condition or disability, for people aged 16 up to state pension age (and after if already claiming).
terms.long: PIP is not about being out of work. It is paid for the extra costs of living with a long-term physical or mental health condition or disability, to people who are working, not working and retired alike. It is not means-tested and not taxable.
terms.why_paid: An assessment looks at how the condition affects 'daily living' (such as preparing food, washing, managing medicines, communicating, making budgeting decisions) and 'mobility' (planning and following journeys, moving around). Each component is awarded at a standard or enhanced rate, or not at all, according to the points scored. The average award reflects how many people have one or both components and at which rate. The 'condition' shown in the data is the main disabling condition recorded, grouped by the medical classification (ICD); mental and behavioural disorders and musculoskeletal conditions are the largest groups.
terms.who: Adults of working age and some older people with a health condition or disability that has lasted, or is expected to last, at least 12 months and affects daily living or mobility. Children get DLA.
terms.amount: Daily living and mobility components at standard or enhanced rate; the weekly amount rises each April with prices.
terms.avoid_blame: A PIP award is the outcome of an assessment of how a condition affects daily life; it is not a reward for not working and many recipients work. The size of an area's PIP caseload tracks how many residents report a disability (see the census comparison).
used_by: Personal Independence Payment cases, per 100 aged 15 to 64

terms.short: Help with the extra costs of disability, now mainly paid for children and to some adults who have not yet moved to PIP.
terms.long: DLA was replaced by PIP for working-age adults from 2013; it continues for children under 16 and for some adults who were awarded it earlier. It has care and mobility components.
terms.why_paid: Awarded for the extra care or mobility needs caused by a disability or health condition, assessed on the effect of the condition.
terms.who: Disabled children and some adults on an existing award.
terms.amount: Care component (three levels) and mobility component (two levels).
terms.avoid_blame: DLA for children is paid to families caring for a disabled child.
used_by: Disability Living Allowance cases in payment (count)
Disability Living Allowance cases in payment, per 100 residents

terms.short: Help for people over state pension age who need care or supervision because of illness or disability.
terms.long: Attendance Allowance is for people who have reached state pension age and need help with personal care or supervision because of a physical or mental disability. It is not means-tested and is not paid for carers.
terms.why_paid: Paid at a lower or higher rate depending on whether the need for help is during the day or night or both.
terms.avoid_blame: Almost all recipients are over state pension age and the payment is for care needs; it is not an out-of-work benefit.
used_by: Attendance Allowance cases in payment, per 100 aged 65 and over

terms.short: A small weekly payment to people who care for someone with a disability for at least 35 hours a week.
terms.long: Carer's Allowance is paid to someone who looks after a person receiving a qualifying disability benefit for at least 35 hours a week, if the carer's earnings are below a limit and they are not in full-time education. It is the lowest-paying of the main benefits.
terms.why_paid: It recognises unpaid care, which saves the state far more than it costs: the person cared for might otherwise need paid care.
terms.who: Unpaid carers meeting the hours and earnings tests (about 1 million cases).
terms.avoid_blame: Carer's Allowance is paid for providing care, not for being out of work, and the amount is far below a wage.
used_by: Carer's Allowance cases in payment, per 100 aged 15 to 64

terms.short: Support for people whose illness or disability limits their ability to work; now closed to new claims in most areas as Universal Credit replaces it.
terms.long: ESA is for people who cannot work, or can only work in a limited way, because of illness or disability. 'New style' ESA depends on National Insurance contributions; 'income-related' ESA is means-tested and is being replaced by Universal Credit. Those still on the older 'legacy' award are counted here; new claimants with limited capability for work are generally on Universal Credit instead.
terms.why_paid: Awarded after the Work Capability Assessment finds that a health condition limits capability for work.
terms.who: People with a health condition or disability who have been assessed.
terms.amount: A basic rate, with extra for those in a support group.
terms.avoid_blame: ESA is for people assessed as too ill or disabled to work; the number on it is falling as people move to UC.
used_by: Employment and Support Allowance cases, per 100 aged 15 to 64

terms.short: The pension paid by the state from state pension age, based on National Insurance contributions or credits.
terms.long: The State Pension is paid to people who have reached state pension age and have enough qualifying National Insurance years. People who reached pension age before April 2016 get the 'basic' pension (and sometimes extra pension); people who reached it after get the 'new State Pension'. It is not means-tested.
terms.why_paid: It is earned: working people pay National Insurance during their working lives, and the State Pension is paid from the contributions of the current working population. The amount reflects the person's National Insurance record, the date they reached pension age, and any protected payment or extra pension.
terms.who: People at or above state pension age with a qualifying record (about 13 million).
terms.amount: A weekly amount that rises each April by the 'triple lock' (the highest of earnings growth, price inflation or 2.5%).
terms.avoid_blame: State Pension is the single biggest benefit (more than half of benefit spending) and is paid for contributions made over a lifetime.
used_by: State Pension recipients, per 100 aged 65 and over

terms.short: A top-up for pensioners on a low income, bringing weekly income up to a minimum level.
terms.long: Pension Credit is a means-tested payment for people over the qualifying age whose income is below a set level. The Guarantee Credit tops income up to the minimum; the Savings Credit rewards some modest savings. It also opens the door to other help (such as Housing Benefit and the Winter Fuel Payment in some years).
terms.why_paid: Because the State Pension alone leaves some people below a minimum income; the amount is the gap.
terms.who: Pensioners with low income and limited savings; many eligible people do not claim.
terms.amount: Whatever tops income up to the minimum.
terms.avoid_blame: Take-up is incomplete: millions of eligible pensioners do not claim, so counts understate need.
used_by: Pension Credit claimants, per 100 aged 65 and over

terms.short: Help paying rent for people on a low income; closed to most working-age new claims because Universal Credit includes housing costs.
terms.long: Housing Benefit helps with rent for people on a low income. For most working-age people the housing element has moved into Universal Credit; Housing Benefit continues mainly for pensioners and for some people in supported, sheltered or temporary accommodation.
terms.why_paid: It meets all or part of rent, depending on income, household size, and the local rent limits.
terms.who: Mostly pensioners and people in supported or temporary housing; tenants only (not owners).
terms.amount: Related to rent and income, with local limits.
terms.avoid_blame: Housing Benefit pays landlords' rent for people who cannot afford it; its amount follows local rents.

terms.short: Children living in families whose income, from benefit and tax-credit records, is below 60% of the typical (median) family income.
terms.long: DWP and HMRC count children aged 0 to 19 in families receiving Universal Credit or tax credits whose reported income is below 60% of the UK median (relative low income), here before housing costs. It is measured from administrative records, so it covers families claiming support, not everyone in poverty.
terms.not_this: It is a measure of family income relative to others, not of hardship in a particular household.
used_by: Children in relative low income families (before housing costs) (count)
Children in relative low income families (before housing costs), per 100 aged 0 to 19

terms.term: National Insurance number (NINo) registrations to adult overseas nationals
terms.short: New National Insurance numbers allocated to non-UK nationals aged 16+ who have come to the UK.
terms.long: Anyone working or claiming benefits in the UK needs a National Insurance number. DWP counts the numbers allocated to adult overseas nationals entering the UK, by nationality group and area of residence. It is an indicator of new arrivals who intend to work, claim or (in some cases) study.
terms.not_this: It is not net migration, not a count of people living here, and it is not a count of benefit claims. Children, many dependants and short stays are not included.
used_by: National Insurance number registrations to adult overseas nationals, 2025/26
NINo registrations to adult overseas nationals, 2023/24 to 2025/26, per 1,000 residents

terms.short: The count of everyone usually living in an area on 21 March 2021.
terms.long: The census asks everyone in England and Wales the same questions on one day, 21 March 2021. 'Usual residents' are people who lived at the address for 12 months or intended to. Scotland and Northern Ireland run separate censuses (not loaded yet). Census figures are a 2021 snapshot taken during Covid restrictions.
terms.not_this: They do not describe the population today: areas change, especially through migration and new housing.

terms.short: The census splits adults into working, looking for work, and neither.
terms.long: Economically active means in work or unemployed. Employed (or 'in employment') people did paid work in the week before census day (including students who worked). Unemployed means not working but looking for work in the last four weeks and available to start within two weeks. Economically inactive people are neither working nor looking: they may be retired, students, looking after home or family, long-term sick or disabled, or other. The unemployment rate is unemployed divided by the economically active, not by everyone.
terms.not_this: 'Economically inactive' is not 'unwilling to work': it includes people who are retired, studying, caring or ill.
used_by: Unemployment rate (unemployed as a share of the economically active)
Aged 16+ long-term sick or disabled (economically inactive)
Aged 16+ looking after home or family

terms.short: People who report a long-term physical or mental health condition or illness that limits their day-to-day activities.
terms.long: In the census, a person is 'disabled' if they say they have a physical or mental health condition or illness lasting or expected to last 12 months or more that reduces their ability to carry out day-to-day activities (a little or a lot), which matches the Equality Act definition. It is self-reported and includes many people who work.
terms.not_this: It is not the same as claiming a disability benefit, and it does not measure how severe a condition is.

terms.short: A person's own rating of their health, from very good to very bad.
terms.long: Self-rated health on a five-point scale. 'Bad or very bad' is a common summary of poor health. Self-rating is influenced by age and expectations.

terms.short: Looking after or helping someone with a long-term illness, disability or old age, without pay.
terms.long: The census asks whether people give unpaid help or support to family, friends or neighbours because of long-term physical or mental ill health or disability, or problems related to old age, and for how many hours a week. Carer's Allowance is paid to only a minority of carers (those caring 35+ hours who meet an earnings limit).
used_by: Providing 50 or more hours of unpaid care a week

terms.term: Born abroad, passports, length of residence and 'migration status'
terms.short: The census measures where people were born, which passports they hold and when they arrived: not their immigration status.
terms.long: 'Born outside the UK' means country of birth is not the UK: it includes British citizens born abroad (such as children of service families), people who have lived here for decades and recent arrivals. 'Passports held' counts each passport a person holds (some hold more than one). 'Length of residence' and 'year of arrival' show how long people born abroad have lived in the UK. None of these shows a person's visa or immigration status.
terms.not_this: The census does not record immigration status, so it cannot say how many people are asylum seekers, refugees, students or workers.
used_by: Born in the Middle East and Asia
Arrived in the UK in the last five years before the census
Arrived in the UK less than two years before the census
Born abroad and resident 10 years or more

terms.short: How a person describes their own ethnic group.
terms.long: Ethnic group is self-identified from a list. It is not nationality, country of birth or religion, and people of the same ethnic group have varied backgrounds.
used_by: White English, Welsh, Scottish, Northern Irish or British
White: Irish, Gypsy or Irish Traveller, Roma, Other White
Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh
Black, Black British, Black Welsh, Caribbean or African

terms.short: A voluntary question: the religion a person says they belong to, or none.
terms.long: The religion question is the only voluntary census question; about 6% of people in England and Wales did not answer. 'Christian' and 'No religion' describe how people identify, not how often they attend a place of worship.
terms.not_this: Religion is not linked to benefit or spending data on this site and should not be read as a cause of any pattern.

terms.short: Whether a household owns its home, rents from a council or housing association, or rents privately.
terms.long: Owned includes owned outright and with a mortgage; shared ownership; social rented (council or housing association); private rented; rent free. It is counted for households, not people.
used_by: Households that own their home (outright or with a mortgage)
Households renting from a council or housing association

terms.short: Highest qualification, current job type and a social class grouping from census answers.
terms.long: Level 4 qualifications and above are degree-level or equivalent. The occupation groups are the nine standard major groups (managers to elementary occupations). NS-SeC (National Statistics Socio-economic Classification) groups people by their job type and employment status, from higher managerial and professional to routine, plus never worked and students.
used_by: Aged 16+ in higher or lower managerial and professional occupations
Aged 16+ in routine or semi-routine occupations
Aged 16+ never worked or long-term unemployed

terms.short: A government ranking of small areas in England by relative deprivation across seven kinds of disadvantage.
terms.long: The English Indices of Deprivation combine income, employment, education, health, crime, barriers to housing and living environment into an index. An authority's 'average score' summarises its small areas; higher means more deprived. 'The most deprived third' orders constituencies or authorities by that score. Constituency scores here are our estimate from authority scores.
terms.not_this: It is relative (an area is ranked against other areas), covers England only, and says nothing about individuals living in the area.
used_by: Deprivation: average IMD score (higher = more deprived; England)

terms.short: Household income adjusted for household size so households of different sizes can be compared.
terms.long: A household of four needs more income than a single person for the same standard of living, so the ONS adjusts income by household size and composition. 'Disposable income' is income after direct taxes and before spending.

terms.short: One of 650 areas each electing an MP; the 2024 boundaries are used.
terms.long: There are 650 constituencies in the UK (543 England, 32 Wales, 57 Scotland, 18 Northern Ireland), redrawn in 2024. A constituency can sit inside one local authority, or be spread across several; a local authority can contain several constituencies. Census figures here are added up from small census areas assigned to the constituency that contains most of each ('best fit').

terms.term: Local authority, council, unitary, district and county
terms.short: The council that runs local services; some areas have one council, others two tiers.
terms.long: A unitary authority, metropolitan district or London borough provides every council service ('all-purpose'). In two-tier areas a county council provides education, social care and highways and a district council provides housing, waste and planning. Comparing spending per head is fair only between all-purpose authorities.

terms.short: Small census areas used as building blocks: about 130 households per output area.
terms.long: Census output areas (about 188,000 in England and Wales) are the smallest areas for which census results are published. Larger groupings are LSOAs and MSOAs. Constituencies and local authorities are built by adding up output areas, which is why their totals match exactly.

terms.short: England's nine regions, the three other nations, and the groupings used by different sources.
terms.long: DWP benefit tables cover Great Britain (England, Wales and Scotland) because Northern Ireland's benefits are devolved. The census tables here cover England and Wales. Council finance returns cover England. Always check which area a total refers to.

terms.short: Payments are placed where the recipient is registered, not where the money is spent.
terms.long: Payments over £25,000, grants and contract awards are matched to a constituency by the recipient's postcode (or the supplier's registered office). A national contractor's head office receives money for work done elsewhere, so this shows where recipients are based, not where services are delivered.

terms.short: All public spending: departments, benefits and pensions, local government and debt interest.
terms.long: TME is the Treasury's measure of total public sector spending. It combines day-to-day and capital spending that departments plan (DEL), demand-led spending like benefits and debt interest (AME), and some accounting adjustments.

terms.short: DEL is spending set in advance within limits; AME is demand-led spending that cannot be planned the same way.
terms.long: Departmental Expenditure Limits (DEL) are budgets set for several years. Annually Managed Expenditure (AME) covers things driven by demand or events, such as State Pension, Universal Credit, PIP and debt interest, which are forecast rather than capped.

terms.term: Cash terms and real terms (2025-26 prices)
terms.short: Cash terms are the pounds of the day; real terms remove price rises to compare over time.
terms.long: £1bn in 2017-18 buys more than £1bn in 2025-26. Real-terms figures here are converted to 2025-26 prices using the Treasury's GDP deflator so spending in different years can be compared.

terms.short: A measure compared with the size of the whole economy.
terms.long: GDP is the value of everything the UK economy produces in a year. 'Spending is 44.5% of GDP' compares spending with the size of the economy, so it can be compared across decades.

terms.term: Borrowing, debt, debt interest and the primary balance
terms.short: Borrowing is the yearly shortfall; debt is the running total; the primary balance ignores interest.
terms.long: Net borrowing is spending minus receipts in a year. Net debt is the stock built up over years. Debt interest is what is paid on that stock. The primary balance is receipts minus spending excluding debt interest: if positive, the government would be reducing debt before interest costs.

terms.term: Funding passed to other public bodies
terms.short: Money one part of government gives to another, such as NHS England or councils.
terms.long: Payments to NHS England, local councils, academy trusts and similar bodies are transfers between public bodies. They are excluded from 'payments to suppliers' totals so the same money is not counted as spent on suppliers.

terms.short: The maximum value stated in a contract notice, not the money actually spent.
terms.long: Contract award notices (and frameworks) state a maximum value. Actual spending is usually lower, and a framework may cover many buyers. The site shows ceilings only as ceilings.

terms.short: What a council spends running services in a year, after income from fees and charges.
terms.long: Net current expenditure is a council's day-to-day spending by service minus service income (fees, charges and some grants counted against services). It excludes capital spending and some financing items. 'Total service expenditure' adds the services; schools funded by the Dedicated Schools Grant are included in education.
terms.not_this: It is not the council's total budget, and spending per head is influenced by age, need, grants and what services the council provides.

terms.term: Council Tax, Band D, precepts and business rates
terms.short: The local property tax; Band D is the standard for comparing areas.
terms.long: Council Tax is set by councils within government limits. 'Average Band D' is the council tax on a Band D home, used to compare areas whatever the mix of home values. Precepts are amounts added by county councils, police, fire and parish councils. Councils also keep part of business rates and receive grants from central government.

terms.short: A person with enough taxable income to be liable to Income Tax; total income includes pay, pensions, savings and profits.
terms.long: HMRC's percentile tables rank people liable to Income Tax (about 37 million) by total income before tax: pay, self-employment profit, pensions, interest and dividends. The 'top 1%' means the top 1% of Income Tax payers, not of all adults.

terms.short: The average rate is total tax divided by total income; the marginal rate applies to the next pound earned.
terms.long: A person paying £10,000 on £50,000 pays an average rate of 20% even though the last pounds were taxed at 40%. Marginal rates also include National Insurance, student loans and the withdrawal of benefits.

terms.short: Contributions from workers (employee) and employers that earn entitlement to some benefits, including the State Pension.
terms.long: Employee NICs are taken from pay; employers pay a separate employer NIC on wages. Both are counted as tax receipts here, grouped by who the law makes liable.

terms.short: HMRC's estimate of tax that should have been paid but was not.
terms.long: The gap is the difference between the tax HMRC estimates is owed and what is collected. It includes evasion, avoidance, error and the hidden economy, and is an estimate with a margin of error.

terms.term: Original, gross, disposable, post-tax and final income (ETB)
terms.short: The ONS 'effects of taxes and benefits' tables follow a household's income through each stage.
terms.long: Original income is earnings, pensions and investment income. Gross income adds cash benefits. Disposable income subtracts direct taxes (Income Tax, National Insurance, Council Tax). Post-tax income subtracts indirect taxes (VAT and duties). Final income adds the value of services received in kind (such as the NHS and schools).

terms.term: Asylum seeker, refugee, grant of protection and grant rate
terms.short: An asylum seeker has asked for protection and is waiting; a refugee has been granted it.
terms.long: A person claiming asylum asks the UK for protection because they fear persecution at home. They are an asylum seeker until the Home Office or a court decides. A grant of protection (refugee status or humanitarian protection) lets them stay. The grant rate is the share of decisions that are grants. Claiming asylum is lawful whatever route a person used to arrive.
terms.not_this: Being refused is not the same as having made a fraudulent claim. Refusals include claims that fail the legal test in good faith.

terms.term: Asylum hotels, dispersal and initial accommodation
terms.short: Housing the Home Office provides to asylum seekers who would otherwise be destitute.
terms.long: Asylum seekers cannot normally work or claim most benefits, so if destitute they may be housed (and given a small cash allowance). Initial accommodation is short-term; dispersal accommodation is longer-term housing in an area; hotels are used when other housing is unavailable. The cost is for housing and support during the time the claim takes to decide.

terms.short: Headcount counts people; full-time equivalent counts full-time posts.
terms.long: Headcount is the number of people employed, whether they work five days or one. Full-time equivalent (FTE) adds up working time: two people each working half a week are 1.0 FTE. FTE is smaller than headcount where part-time work is common (the NHS is about 1.54 million people and 1.37 million FTE). A person with two jobs can be counted twice in headcount. Each workforce figure on this site names which one it is.

terms.term: Public sector employment (ONS) and who is not a civil servant
terms.category: Who is paid by the state
terms.short: Everyone employed by government bodies and publicly owned companies: about 6.2 million people, of whom 0.56 million are civil servants.
terms.long: The ONS counts people employed in central government (civil servants, the armed forces, NHS England and other national bodies), local government (councils, council-run schools, police staff), and public corporations (for example Network Rail and the BBC). Most public servants people think of are NOT civil servants: nurses, doctors, teachers, police officers, firefighters, soldiers and council staff are employed by NHS trusts, schools, forces or councils, not by a government department. The ONS industry cut (NHS, education, police, armed forces, public administration) and the sector cut (central, local, public corporations) are two ways of dividing the same total.
terms.not_this: Public sector employment is not the number of people paid from taxes: contractors, suppliers' staff, pensioners, and people on benefits are outside it.

terms.category: Who is paid by the state
terms.short: The national pay scale for NHS staff other than doctors and dentists: Band 1 (lowest) to Band 9 (highest), plus Very Senior Managers.
terms.long: Each non-medical NHS job is placed in a band by a national job-evaluation system; the band sets a pay range with steps for experience. Typical jobs: Bands 1 to 3 are porters, cleaners and healthcare assistants; Band 4 assistant practitioners and administrators; Band 5 newly qualified nurses and physiotherapists; Band 6 experienced nurses and specialists; Band 7 senior nurses and team leaders; Bands 8 and 9 senior managers and consultants in scientific roles. Doctors and dentists are paid on separate national contracts. A band shows the level of a job, not how much any individual works.

terms.short: A temporary reduction of someone's Universal Credit because they did not meet a work requirement, usually without good reason.
terms.long: If a claimant who has work requirements misses an appointment, does not apply for jobs they agreed to, or leaves work voluntarily, DWP can reduce the payment for a fixed period. DWP's data flag, for every claimant, whether a sanction was applied in the month. The share depends on who is counted: of all claimants it is small (about 1 in 80), of claimants who have work requirements it is about 1 in 30. Sanctions can be challenged and some are overturned. Claimants with no work requirements (for example because of health or caring) cannot be sanctioned for work-search failures.
terms.not_this: A sanction rate is not the share of claimants who ever break the rules, and a lower rate does not show better behaviour: it can reflect how DWP applies its rules.

terms.term: Benefit combinations (people claiming more than one benefit)
terms.short: How many different benefits the same person receives at once, such as Universal Credit with PIP, or State Pension with Pension Credit.
terms.long: DWP links its records to count the people who receive one benefit and those who receive two or more together. Combinations show that the totals for each benefit (which add to more than the number of claimants) overlap: a disabled person on Universal Credit may also receive PIP, a pensioner may receive State Pension, Pension Credit and Attendance Allowance. The data cover England and Wales.
